doc.title: Ray Conniff interviewed by Monk Rowe, San Diego, California, February 14, 1998

title: Moving to Polygram and arranging 'I Love Movies'
summary: After 40 years with Columbia, Conniff signed with Polygram and explains how he picks ten of 30 movie themes and sketches ideas at the piano, as with 'Star Wars'.

story.theme_name: Jazz musicians in the movies and film scoring
story.community_name: Jazz musicians on film and studio scoring

blocks.x: And your records have been all around the world. I wanted to ask you as we wrap up here, let’s suppose, I think one song that you didn’t pick on here, let’s say you were going to do an arrangement on, are you familiar with the song from “The Lion King,” “Can You Feel The Love Tonight?” Let’s suppose you wanted to give that your treatment. How do you, when you sit down, do you sit down at a keyboard, or do you just think about it in your head, what am I going to do with this particular song? How exactly is it going to start?

By the way, I don’t know if you know my background, but you might notice, this is with a different label, this is my first CD with Polygram. And I’m quite excited about it, because it brings out an answer to your question. When we did the music for this, the fellow that asked me to come with Polygram after being with Columbia Records which became CBS Records which became SONY Music, I outlasted — 40 years I was with the company — I outlasted three name changes and two buyouts. But anyway this fellow that is head of Polygram, the international department, was with SONY Music and he came to a concert, came backstage, “Ray, why don’t you come on Polygram.” He says, “how are things going with SONY?” I says, “oh they take me for granted after 40 years, they don’t promote.” He says, “come with me, I’ll promote you.” So he’s been doing, he sent this kit out. So anyway, when we first met about what I should do, which answers your question, I said, “well what do you think we should do for a first album?” And he came up with the “I Love Movies” idea, you know with the heart for the love. And he said, “I’m going to send you a cassette of not ten — we were going to put ten songs originally, it wound up twelve. He said, “I’ll send you not ten, but I want to send you about 30 songs of movie themes, because he says, I want you to go through them.” And he says, “what I’ve noticed about when Ray Conniff does an arrangement of a song, it kind of becomes your song in a way, because it’s different than it was any other time anyone else did it.” He says, “I want you to listen to 30, and pick ten that you can make your sound on.” And that’s the way I did it. So I took the 30 and went through all 30, and I listened to each one quite a bit. And I will first work with the sheet music and first I’ll listen to the theme as it was done in the movie, like the “Star Wars” theme by John Williams, or “Can You Read

My Mind.” And then I will get the sheet music out and sit at the piano and just kind of see what comes to me. And I’ll make notes up on the piano part of ideas that came to me on that. And I went through all 30, and I make kind of pencil notes on the piano bar. Or I might grab a piece of manuscript or something if there wasn’t room to put it on the piano part, and I’ll put “Star Wars” on the outside and scribble out a little line that I have. Like on “Star Wars” what comes to me is that I started fiddling with the chords of “Star Wars,” and I happened to be in G, which “Somewhere My Love” was in. And I’d just come from a rehearsal with the singers and we’d been rehearsing that, and I started playing [scats], which is the same as the piano background of “Somewhere My Love.” I says hey you know what? That would work on this. And I just took the G, D, G, B, G, D, G, D, B, C [scats]. And used the “Somewhere My Love” background piano pattern with “Star Wars.” And [scats] I did a much slower tempo. And used the trombones and men and low saxes for the theme [scats]. And so I’d write that idea down, and go through all 30. Then I’ll go back through and I will think about, I’m leaving it up to him to send me 30 that he says to him it doesn’t make any difference which ten I pick. And I will think though about you know, “Star Wars” had a lot of publicity. You know it had a big push. So if I can fit in with songs that have had — like if now I was doing it I’d certainly have put some stuff from “Titanic” in you know, it’s so big, that people are going to see songs from “Titanic” in the CD and they’re going to lean towards that. So I’ll lean that way a little. But on the whole, I’ll get the best ten ideas and those are the ones that will wind up in the album.
